options.content: The release of electrons from a heated metal surface
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The release of light from a very hot metal
options.rationale: That is incandescence.

options.content: The release of heat by electrons moving in a wire
options.rationale: That is heating by a current, not emission.

options.content: The release of positive ions from a heated gas
options.rationale: Thermionic emission releases electrons, not ions.

explanation: When a metal is heated strongly, some free electrons gain enough energy to escape from its surface.

stem: Why must a cathode-ray tube contain a vacuum?

options.content: So electrons do not hit gas molecules and scatter or slow down
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: To keep the filament cool so it lasts much longer
options.rationale: The filament must be hot.

options.content: To make the fluorescent screen glow more brightly
options.rationale: The screen glows where electrons hit it.

options.content: To give the electrons their negative charge as they leave
options.rationale: Electrons are always negative.

explanation: Gas molecules would stop and scatter the electrons, so the tube is evacuated.

stem: What is the job of the anode in an electron gun?

options.content: To emit the electrons that go on to form the beam
options.rationale: The hot cathode emits them.

options.content: To attract and speed up electrons, which pass through as a beam
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: To heat the cathode filament up to a high temperature
options.rationale: A separate low-voltage supply does that.

options.content: To deflect the beam sideways and up and down on the screen
options.rationale: Deflecting plates or coils do that.

explanation: The anode is held at a high positive p.d.; it accelerates the electrons, and its central hole lets a narrow beam through.

stem: An electron beam passing between two charged parallel plates bends towards the positive plate.
explanation: Electrons are negative, so they are attracted towards the positive plate.

stem: An electron beam travels to the right between two horizontal plates. The lower plate is positive and the upper plate is negative. How is the beam deflected?

options.content: Upwards, towards the negative plate
options.rationale: Electrons are repelled by the negative plate.

options.content: Into the page
options.rationale: The electric force is towards a plate.

options.content: It is not deflected.
options.rationale: There is a force on the charged electrons.

options.content: Downwards, towards the positive plate
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: The negative electrons are attracted to the lower, positive plate, so the beam curves downwards.

stem: An electron beam travels to the right through a magnetic field directed out of the page. Which way is the beam deflected?

options.content: Downwards
options.rationale: Remember the current is opposite to the electrons' motion.

options.content: Into the page
options.rationale: The force is at right angles to the field.

options.content: Out of the page
options.rationale: The force is at right angles to the field.

options.content: Upwards
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: The conventional current is to the left. Left hand: first finger out of the page, second finger to the left: the thumb points upwards.
hints: Use Fleming's left-hand rule with the current opposite to the electrons' motion.

stem: What makes the spot on the screen of a cathode-ray oscilloscope visible?

options.content: The electrons themselves are hot and glow as they fly.
options.rationale: Electrons are not seen; the coating glows.

options.content: The screen's fluorescent coating glows where electrons hit it.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The vacuum inside the tube glows faintly.
options.rationale: A vacuum cannot glow.

options.content: The deflecting plates give out light as they charge up and steer the beam.
options.rationale: The plates steer the beam; they do not glow.

explanation: A fluorescent material on the inside of the screen gives out light where the beam hits it.

stem: On a CRO with the Y-gain set at 5 V/div, the peaks of an a.c. trace are 2.4 divisions above the centre line. What is the peak p.d.?
hints: Multiply the number of divisions by the Y-gain.

stem: A CRO's time-base is set at 2 ms/div. One complete wave of a signal occupies 5.0 divisions. Calculate the frequency of the signal.
hints: Find the period first, in seconds.

stem: In a cathode-ray oscilloscope, what does the time-base do?

options.content: It moves the spot up and down in step with the p.d. at the Y-input terminals
options.rationale: That is the Y-input and Y-plates.

options.content: It sweeps the spot steadily across the screen from left to right.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: It heats the cathode.
options.rationale: No.

options.content: It focuses the beam.
options.rationale: No.

explanation: The time-base drives the X-plates, moving the spot across the screen at a steady rate so that signals are drawn against time.

stem: A steady d.c. p.d. is connected to the Y-input of a CRO with the time-base switched on. What is seen on the screen?

options.content: A wave moving across the screen
options.rationale: A wave needs a changing p.d.

options.content: A vertical line through the centre
options.rationale: That is an a.c. input with the time-base off.

options.content: A horizontal line moved up or down from the centre
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Nothing at all, as a steady d.c. input cannot be shown
options.rationale: The spot is still visible.

explanation: The steady p.d. shifts the spot a fixed distance up (or down) while the time-base sweeps it across, drawing a horizontal line.
hints: The p.d. does not change, but the spot still moves across the screen.

stem: Match each part of a cathode-ray tube with its job.

right.content: Deflect the beam up and down
Accelerates the electrons into a beam

explanation: Cathode: emits. Anode: accelerates. Y-plates: vertical deflection. Screen: glows.

stem: A signal from a microphone is displayed on a CRO with the Y-gain at 0.5 V/div and the time-base at 1 ms/div. The peaks are 3.0 divisions above the centre line, and 4 complete waves fill 10 divisions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the peak p.d. of the signal.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the period of the signal in milliseconds.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the frequency of the sound.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The sound becomes louder but keeps the same pitch. How does the trace change?

options.content: There are more waves across the width of the screen.
options.rationale: That would be a higher pitch.

options.content: There are fewer waves on the screen.
options.rationale: That would be a lower pitch.

options.content: The waves are taller, with the same spacing.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The trace becomes a flat line.
options.rationale: No.

parts.explanation: Loudness depends on amplitude (height); pitch depends on frequency (spacing).

explanation: Divisions × Y-gain gives p.d.; divisions × time-base gives time; f = 1/T.
hints: Convert milliseconds to seconds before finding the frequency.
